newsitem.title: USA: Campaign '96 is over but Kemp keeps running.
newsitem.headline: Campaign '96 is over but Kemp keeps running.

text.p: The 1996 presidential election may be over but defeated Republican vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp has not stopped running.

Barely pausing for breath after the campaign, Kemp is now travelling the country, putting the pieces into place for his own assault on the White House in 2000, spreading his ideas of racial equality and inclusiveness with the passion of an itinerant preacher.

"We're spending 25 days a month on the road, travelling very aggressively, laying the groundwork for a potential candidacy. We wouldn't be out here doing this if he wasn't taking this very seriously," a Kemp aide said.

Wednesday found Kemp in Buffalo, which he represented in Congress for 18 years and where he was quarterback of the Buffalo Bills football team for 10 years before that. Kemp was in town to speak at a fund-raising event for the local Erie County Republican Party but he also found time to hold a news conference and give 15 quick interviews with local media.

The message: "I believe with all my heart that there is a struggle going on for the heart and soul of the Republican Party. That party must be inclusive, not exclusive, it must be progressive and conservative, not reactionary and conservative.

"The Republican Party must learn to persuade people of our values, not impose those values. We should be using persuasion and example instead of the imposition of some type of a one-size-fits-all model for the values debate."

When asked about his presidential ambitions, as he is at virtually every stop, Kemp has a standard answer: "The American people have just been through a very vigorous campaign. I enjoyed it, loved it. It whetted my appetite but I'm not going to do anything until after the 1998 (congressional) elections."

Still, Kemp recently set up a political action committee and is raising money to finance his travels. By supporting Republican congressional candidates next year, he will be able to forge critical alliances for his own presidential bid.

Kemp's message, delivered with true conviction, is certainly an unusual one for a Republican. At the Erie County event he wound up with a passage that seemed self-consciously modelled on the style of the late black civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.

"We must lift the weight of oppression of poverty. We must lift the weight of oppression of racism. We must lift the weight of oppression of anti-Semitism. We must lift the weight of oppression of unemployment and joblessness. We must lift the weight of oppression on the American family. We must be a party of emancipation. We must be a party of liberation. We must be a party of equality.

"We must take our message to the ghetto, we must take it to the barrio, we must take it to the immigrant. We must take it to every corner of this country," Kemp declared, as the audience drowned out his final words with applause.
Later, in an interview with Reuters, he said he regarded his adversaries in the Republican Party as those who could not recognise how the world had changed since the Cold War ended.

"There are certainly goblins out there to be slain. America cannot be xenophobic. It must be in a borderless world to capital and ideas. We've got to work towards a borderless world to trade, to human rights, to the struggle for an end to oppressive conditions wherever they exist," he said.

Kemp was criticised by some Republicans during last year's election for campaigning in black inner cities when it was clear most of the black vote would go to President Clinton. He was also lambasted by his own party for his performance in a debate against Vice President Al Gore, which Kemp now acknowledges he lost.

"People wanted me to be the attack dog of the right. I'm not a pit bull. I'm not an attack dog. For good or bad, I am a happy warrior. I lost the debate but I've lost football games and I've come back and learned from my mistakes. I think I can learn from the mistake of losing to Al Gore in that debate," he said.
